Chapter 8 — Navigating Difficult Conversations and Correcting Misinformation.
Even when you’ve built a strong commitment to truth, misinformation will still pop up from time to time. So, what do you do when someone you know—maybe a friend online or a family member at dinner—shares something that just isn’t true?
Well, correcting misinformation can feel tricky. People get attached to their beliefs, and if you come at them head-on, it can actually make things worse. The goal isn’t to “win” the argument. Instead, it’s about opening up a space where both of you can reflect and maybe learn something new together.
Here’s where empathy really matters. Before you even think about correcting someone, it helps to ask yourself—why do they believe this? Is it fear? Loyalty to a group? Or maybe just wanting some certainty in a confusing world?
When you start by listening, you show respect—and that alone can calm things down and make honest conversation possible.
There are a few gentle ways you can help someone see things differently:
First, try asking questions. Instead of saying, “That’s wrong,” you might ask, “Where did you hear that?” or, “What makes you think that’s true?” It’s a friendly way to invite a real conversation, not a debate.
You can also share how you reached your own understanding. Maybe you looked up several sources, or asked yourself tough questions before forming an opinion.
And when you do offer evidence, focus on being curious, not superior. Share links, data, or experts’ opinions in a way that says, “Hey, I found this interesting—what do you think?”
It also helps to highlight what you both care about. You might say, “I know we both want what’s best for our community,” or, “We both care about being accurate.” Finding that common ground can really shift the tone.
Picture this: you’re at a family dinner, and someone brings up a viral rumor. Instead of shutting them down, you might gently ask where they heard it, share what you discovered, and thank them for caring about the issue. Even if they don’t change their mind right away, you’ve planted a seed for future reflection.
But sometimes, you’ll notice a conversation isn’t going anywhere. That’s okay. Not every discussion is worth pursuing. In those moments, the best thing you can do is model truthfulness—and trust that, over time, others might follow your lead.
So, by approaching these moments with empathy, patience, and humility, you really can help slow the spread of misinformation—without harming your relationships.
